question_en: How many layers does the OSI reference model have?
explanation_en: The OSI model has seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation and Application. The TCP/IP model is usually described with four layers, which is the common distractor.

question_en: Which OSI layer is responsible for routing packets from the source host to the destination host across multiple networks?
explanation_en: Routing and logical (IP) addressing belong to the Network layer (layer 3). The Data Link layer delivers frames only within one physical network segment.

question_en: Segmentation of application data, end-to-end error recovery and flow control between two hosts are functions of the:
explanation_en: The Transport layer (layer 4, e.g. TCP) breaks data into segments and provides process-to-process reliable delivery. The Data Link layer also does error detection, but only hop-to-hop, not end-to-end.

question_en: The protocol data unit (PDU) handled at the Data Link layer is called a:
explanation_en: Data Link layer PDU = frame; Network layer = packet (datagram); Transport layer = segment; Physical layer = bits.

question_en: Data compression, encryption and conversion between character encodings (e.g. ASCII to Unicode) are services of which OSI layer?
explanation_en: The Presentation layer (layer 6) is the 'translator' of the OSI model: it handles data format, compression and encryption. The Session layer manages dialogues, not data representation.

question_en: Which OSI layer establishes, maintains, synchronises and terminates the dialogue between two communicating applications?
explanation_en: Dialogue control, synchronisation points and session management are Session layer (layer 5) functions.

question_en: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Data Link layer?
explanation_en: Logical addressing (IP addresses) is a Network layer function. Framing, MAC addressing, error detection and media access control are all Data Link layer responsibilities.

question_en: The Session, Presentation and Application layers of the OSI model together correspond to which single layer of the TCP/IP model?
explanation_en: The four-layer TCP/IP model merges OSI layers 5, 6 and 7 into one Application layer, and merges OSI layers 1 and 2 into the Network Access (Link) layer.

question_en: ICMP, the protocol used by the ping command to report errors and reachability, operates at which layer?
explanation_en: ICMP is carried inside IP packets and is considered part of the Network/Internet layer along with IP, ARP and IGMP.

question_en: When data moves down the protocol stack at the sending host, the correct order of encapsulation is:
explanation_en: Transport layer creates segments, Network layer wraps them in packets, Data Link layer wraps packets in frames, and the Physical layer transmits bits. Option 4 is the de-encapsulation order at the receiver.

question_en: Which networking device can operate at all seven layers of the OSI model, translating between entirely different protocol suites?
explanation_en: A gateway performs protocol conversion and may work up to the Application layer. A switch works at layer 2, a bridge at layer 2 and a router at layer 3.

question_en: In the TCP/IP model, the layer that combines the functions of the OSI Physical and Data Link layers is the:
explanation_en: The Network Access or Link layer of TCP/IP handles hardware addressing, framing and physical transmission, i.e. OSI layers 1 and 2. The Internet layer corresponds to OSI layer 3.

question_en: The address used by the Transport layer to deliver data to the correct application process on a host is the:
explanation_en: Port numbers identify processes (services) on a host. MAC addresses are Data Link addresses and IP addresses are Network layer addresses.

question_en: In which topology is every node connected by its own cable to a central device such as a hub or switch?
explanation_en: Star topology uses a central connecting device. It is the most common LAN topology today because one cable fault isolates only one node.

question_en: A fully connected mesh network has 10 computers. How many point-to-point links are required?
explanation_en: A full mesh of n nodes needs n(n−1)/2 links = 10×9/2 = 45. Option 4 counts each link twice (n(n−1)).

question_en: In which topology does data travel in one direction from node to node, and a single node or cable failure can bring down the entire network unless a dual ring is used?
explanation_en: In a ring, each node is connected to exactly two neighbours and data (often a token) circulates in one direction, so one break can disable the whole ring.

question_en: A bus topology requires a terminator at each end of the main cable in order to:
explanation_en: Terminators absorb the signal at the ends of the backbone cable so that it does not bounce back and corrupt new transmissions.

question_en: Which topology offers the highest fault tolerance and privacy but also the highest cabling cost?
explanation_en: Mesh has dedicated links between every pair of nodes, so there are always alternative paths and traffic is not shared, but the number of cables and ports grows rapidly with n.

question_en: In a full mesh network of 8 devices, how many I/O ports must each device have, and what is the total number of links?
explanation_en: Each device connects to the other n−1 = 7 devices, so it needs 7 ports. Total links = n(n−1)/2 = 8×7/2 = 28.

question_en: A hierarchical topology in which several star networks are connected to a linear backbone is called a:
explanation_en: Tree topology combines star groups joined through a bus backbone; it is widely used in large buildings and campus networks.

question_en: In a star topology, what is the effect of a failure of the central hub, and of a failure of a single cable?

options.en: Both bring the whole network down
Hub failure brings the whole network down; a cable failure isolates only one node
Hub failure isolates one node; cable failure brings the whole network down

explanation_en: The hub is a single point of failure, but each node has its own cable, so a cable break affects only that node. This is why star is easy to troubleshoot.

question_en: Which transmission medium carries data as pulses of light and is immune to electromagnetic interference?
explanation_en: Optical fibre transmits light through a glass or plastic core using total internal reflection, so electrical noise cannot affect it and it supports the highest bandwidth over long distances.

question_en: The two wires of each pair in a twisted-pair cable are twisted around each other mainly to:

options.en: Reduce crosstalk and external electromagnetic interference

explanation_en: Twisting makes both wires pick up nearly equal noise, which cancels out at the receiver (differential signalling), reducing crosstalk and EMI.

question_en: Which cable has a central copper conductor surrounded by an insulating layer, a braided metallic shield and an outer plastic jacket?
explanation_en: This layered construction describes coaxial cable, used in cable TV and older Ethernet (10BASE2/10BASE5). UTP has no metallic shield and fibre has a glass core.

question_en: The connector normally used to terminate Cat 5e / Cat 6 twisted-pair Ethernet cables is:
explanation_en: RJ45 is the 8-pin connector for Ethernet twisted-pair cables. RJ11 is for telephone lines, BNC for coaxial cable and SC/ST/LC for optical fibre.

question_en: Which statement correctly contrasts single-mode and multimode optical fibre?

options.en: Single-mode has a larger core and uses LEDs; multimode uses lasers for long distances
Single-mode has a very thin core, is usually driven by a laser and supports longer distances; multimode has a wider core and is used for shorter runs
Both have identical cores; they differ only in jacket colour
Multimode can carry only one wavelength while single-mode carries many

explanation_en: Single-mode fibre (core ≈ 8–10 µm) carries a single light path with very low dispersion, so it works over tens of kilometres. Multimode (core ≈ 50–62.5 µm) allows many paths, causing modal dispersion, so it suits short campus/building links.

question_en: Which of the following is an unguided (wireless) transmission medium?
explanation_en: Guided media use a physical conductor (copper or glass). Microwave, radio waves and infrared travel through free space and are unguided media.

question_en: A geostationary communication satellite appears fixed above one point on the equator because it orbits at a height of approximately:
explanation_en: At about 35,786 km (≈36,000 km) a satellite's orbital period equals the Earth's rotation period (24 h), so it stays over the same spot; this is why a fixed dish antenna works.

question_en: Infrared communication (as used in TV remote controls) is limited because infrared signals:

options.en: Need a licence from the government
Cannot pass through walls and require line of sight

explanation_en: Infrared waves are blocked by opaque objects, so they work only over short, unobstructed distances, which also makes them secure within a room.

question_en: In the Ethernet designation 100BASE-TX, what do '100', 'BASE' and 'T' indicate respectively?
explanation_en: The number is the data rate in Mbps, BASE means baseband (the whole cable carries one digital signal) and T stands for twisted pair; F would mean fibre and 2/5 referred to thin/thick coaxial lengths.

question_en: Compared with unshielded twisted pair (UTP), shielded twisted pair (STP):

options.en: Has a metallic foil or braid that gives better protection against EMI but makes it costlier and bulkier
Uses glass fibres instead of copper

explanation_en: STP adds a shield around the pairs to resist electromagnetic interference, at the cost of price, weight and ease of installation. UTP is the usual choice for office LANs.

question_en: A hub forwards every incoming signal to all of its ports and operates at the ______ layer of the OSI model.
explanation_en: A hub is a multi-port repeater: it regenerates electrical signals without reading addresses, so it belongs to layer 1 and creates one large collision domain.

question_en: A switch forwards a frame only to the port on which the destination is located. To do this it maintains a table of:
explanation_en: A switch is a layer-2 device; it learns the source MAC address of each frame and builds a MAC (CAM) address table that maps addresses to ports. Routers use IP addresses.

question_en: A router makes its forwarding decision by examining the:

options.en: Source MAC address of the frame
Destination IP address of the packet
Destination port number of the segment

explanation_en: Routers work at the Network layer and consult a routing table using the destination IP address. Switches use MAC addresses and firewalls may look at port numbers.

question_en: A device that connects two LAN segments and filters traffic by MAC address, thereby dividing one collision domain into two, is called a:
explanation_en: A bridge is a two-port layer-2 device that forwards frames between segments only when needed; a switch is essentially a multi-port bridge. A repeater does not filter anything.

question_en: Twenty-four PCs are connected to a single 24-port switch, which is connected to a router. How many collision domains and broadcast domains does the switch create among the PCs?
explanation_en: Each switch port is its own collision domain (24), but a switch forwards broadcasts to all ports, so all PCs share one broadcast domain. Only a router (or VLANs) separates broadcast domains; a hub would give 1 collision domain.

question_en: To connect an organisation's IPX-based legacy network to a TCP/IP network, converting between the two protocol stacks, the appropriate device is a:
explanation_en: A gateway translates between different protocol architectures and can operate up to the Application layer; the other devices work within a single protocol family.

question_en: A modem is required for a dial-up or DSL connection because it:

options.en: Converts digital signals of the computer to analog signals for the telephone line and back
Blocks viruses coming from the Internet
Increases the clock speed of the processor

explanation_en: MODEM = MOdulator-DEModulator. It modulates digital data onto an analog carrier for transmission and demodulates the received signal.

question_en: The MAC address burnt into a Network Interface Card (NIC) is:

options.en: 32 bits long, written in dotted decimal
48 bits long, written as 12 hexadecimal digits
128 bits long, written in hexadecimal groups

explanation_en: A MAC address is 48 bits (6 bytes), e.g. 3C:5A:B4:12:9F:01; the first 3 bytes identify the manufacturer (OUI). 32-bit dotted decimal describes IPv4 and 128-bit hex describes IPv6.

question_en: Which device simply regenerates and retimes a weakened signal so that it can travel a longer distance on the same network?
explanation_en: A repeater is a layer-1 device that extends the physical length of a network by amplifying/regenerating the signal; it does not look at addresses.

question_en: The Sales and Accounts departments are on the same switched LAN and broadcast traffic from one department is slowing the other. Which solution would confine broadcasts to each department?

options.en: Replace the switch with a hub
Add a repeater between the departments
Separate the departments with a router or configure VLANs on the switch
Install a faster NIC in every PC

explanation_en: Broadcast domains are bounded by routers (layer 3) or by VLANs on a managed switch. Hubs and repeaters enlarge the collision domain and do nothing to limit broadcasts.

question_en: A wireless access point (AP) is used to:

options.en: Convert optical signals to electrical signals
Connect Wi-Fi client devices to a wired LAN
Replace the need for a router on the Internet

explanation_en: An access point bridges the wireless (802.11) medium and the wired Ethernet LAN; home 'Wi-Fi routers' combine an AP, a switch and a router in one box.

question_en: The IPv4 address 172.16.5.4 belongs to which address class?
explanation_en: The first octet 172 lies in the range 128–191, which is Class B. Class A is 1–126 and Class C is 192–223.

question_en: What is the default subnet mask of a Class C IPv4 address?
explanation_en: Class C uses the first 24 bits for the network, so the default mask is 255.255.255.0 (/24). 255.255.0.0 is the Class B default.

question_en: Which of the following is the IPv4 loopback address used to test the TCP/IP stack on the local machine?
explanation_en: The whole 127.0.0.0/8 block is reserved for loopback and 127.0.0.1 is the conventional address. 192.168.0.1 is a private address and 255.255.255.255 is the limited broadcast.

question_en: IPv4 addresses whose first octet lies between 224 and 239 belong to Class D and are used for:
explanation_en: Class D (224.0.0.0–239.255.255.255) is reserved for multicast groups. Class E (240–255) is the experimental class.

question_en: The subnet mask written in CIDR notation as /26 is equivalent to:
explanation_en: /26 means 26 one-bits: 24 bits give 255.255.255 and the remaining 2 bits in the last octet give 128 + 64 = 192. /25 is .128 and /27 is .224.

question_en: How many usable host addresses are available in a subnet with prefix /27?
explanation_en: Host bits = 32 − 27 = 5, so 2^5 = 32 addresses. Subtracting the network and broadcast addresses gives 32 − 2 = 30 usable hosts.

question_en: A host has the address 10.1.1.130 with mask 255.255.255.128. What is the broadcast address of its subnet?
explanation_en: Block size = 256 − 128 = 128, so the subnets are .0–.127 and .128–.255. Host .130 lies in the second block, whose last address 10.1.1.255 is the broadcast; .128 is that subnet's network address.

question_en: The Class C network 192.168.1.0 is subnetted with prefix /28. How many subnets are created and how many usable hosts does each have?
explanation_en: From the default /24, 4 bits are borrowed: 2^4 = 16 subnets. 4 host bits remain: 2^4 − 2 = 14 usable hosts per subnet.

question_en: The prefix /20 corresponds to which dotted-decimal subnet mask?
explanation_en: /20 = 16 bits (255.255) plus 4 more one-bits in the third octet: 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 = 240. Hence 255.255.240.0.

question_en: How many usable host addresses does a /22 network provide?
explanation_en: Host bits = 32 − 22 = 10, giving 2^10 = 1024 addresses; removing the network and broadcast addresses leaves 1022 usable hosts.

question_en: Which of the following IPv4 addresses is a private (RFC 1918) address that is not routed on the public Internet?
explanation_en: Private ranges are 10.0.0.0/8, 172.16.0.0–172.31.255.255 and 192.168.0.0/16. 172.20.x.x falls in the 172.16–31 block; 172.32 and 192.169 are just outside the private ranges.

question_en: A Windows PC that cannot reach a DHCP server automatically assigns itself an address such as 169.254.23.7. This address range is called:
explanation_en: 169.254.0.0/16 is the link-local range used by Automatic Private IP Addressing when DHCP fails; it only works on the local segment.

question_en: A default Class B network (mask 255.255.0.0) can have at most how many usable hosts?
explanation_en: Class B leaves 16 host bits: 2^16 = 65,536 addresses minus 2 (network and broadcast) = 65,534. 16,777,214 is the Class A figure and 254 is Class C.

question_en: What is the network (subnet) address of the host 192.168.10.77/26?
explanation_en: A /26 mask is 255.255.255.192, block size 64. The subnets in the last octet are 0, 64, 128, 192; 77 falls in 64–127, so the network address is 192.168.10.64 (broadcast 192.168.10.127).

question_en: An organisation has the Class C block 200.10.5.0/24 and needs at least 6 subnets. Using the smallest suitable mask, what is the mask and the number of usable hosts per subnet?
explanation_en: 2 borrowed bits give only 4 subnets, so 3 bits are needed (2^3 = 8 ≥ 6). Mask = /27 = 255.255.255.224, leaving 5 host bits: 2^5 − 2 = 30 hosts per subnet.

question_en: With subnet mask 255.255.255.240, which pair of hosts lies in the SAME subnet?
explanation_en: Block size = 256 − 240 = 16, so subnets are .0–.15, .16–.31, .32–.47, .48–.63. Both .18 and .29 fall in .16–.31; every other pair straddles a block boundary.

question_en: The four networks 192.168.0.0/24, 192.168.1.0/24, 192.168.2.0/24 and 192.168.3.0/24 are to be advertised as one summary (supernet) route. The summary route is:
explanation_en: Four contiguous /24 networks = 2^2, so 2 bits are removed from the prefix: /24 − 2 = /22. The third octets 0–3 share the first 6 bits (000000xx), giving 192.168.0.0/22.

question_en: What is the length of an IPv6 address?
explanation_en: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits and MAC addresses are 48 bits.

question_en: An IPv4 address is written in dotted-decimal notation as four numbers. Each of these numbers can range from:
explanation_en: Each of the four parts is one octet (8 bits), so its value ranges from 0 to 2^8 − 1 = 255. That is why an address such as 192.168.300.1 is invalid.

question_en: The theoretical total number of IPv4 addresses is approximately:
explanation_en: IPv4 uses 32 bits, so there are 2^32 ≈ 4.29 billion addresses. 3.4 × 10^38 (2^128) is the IPv6 address space, which is why IPv6 was introduced.

question_en: Which of the following is a correctly written IPv6 address?
explanation_en: The double colon (::) may replace one run of zero groups and can appear only once, and only hexadecimal digits 0–9 and a–f are allowed. The second option uses :: twice and the third contains the non-hex letter g.

question_en: The IPv6 loopback address is written as:
explanation_en: In IPv6 the loopback is 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1, abbreviated ::1. 127.0.0.1 is the IPv4 loopback; FF02::1 is the all-nodes multicast and FE80:: begins link-local addresses.

question_en: Which type of address exists in IPv4 but has been removed in IPv6?
explanation_en: IPv6 defines unicast, multicast and anycast addresses only; the functions of broadcast are carried out using multicast groups such as FF02::1.

question_en: Which statement correctly compares the IPv4 and IPv6 headers?

options.en: IPv6 header is variable while IPv4 header is fixed at 40 bytes
Both headers are fixed at 20 bytes
IPv4 header is variable (20–60 bytes); IPv6 base header is fixed at 40 bytes
IPv6 header contains a header checksum, IPv4 does not

explanation_en: IPv4 has a 20-byte minimum header that can grow to 60 bytes with options, while IPv6 uses a simplified fixed 40-byte base header with extension headers. IPv6 removed the header checksum to speed up routing.

question_en: The purpose of the Time To Live (TTL) field in an IPv4 packet is to:

options.en: Record the time at which the packet was created
Stop a packet from circulating endlessly; each router decrements it and discards the packet at 0
Give the priority of the packet in a router queue
Indicate how long a TCP connection may remain idle

explanation_en: Every router reduces TTL by 1 and drops the packet when it reaches 0, preventing routing loops from flooding the network. The traceroute command exploits this behaviour. IPv6 calls the same field Hop Limit.

question_en: Which transport-layer protocol is connection-oriented and guarantees reliable, in-order delivery of data?
explanation_en: TCP sets up a connection, numbers segments, uses acknowledgements and retransmission, so delivery is reliable and ordered. UDP is connectionless and gives no such guarantee; IP and ICMP are network-layer protocols.

question_en: The correct sequence of segments in the TCP three-way handshake is:
explanation_en: The client sends SYN, the server replies SYN-ACK, and the client confirms with ACK; the connection is then established. FIN is used to close a connection, not to open one.

question_en: Which application is generally best served by UDP rather than TCP?

options.en: Live voice call over the Internet (VoIP)

explanation_en: Real-time voice tolerates the loss of a few packets but not the delay caused by retransmission, so UDP's low overhead suits it. Downloads, e-mail and banking pages need every byte to arrive correctly, so they use TCP.

question_en: What are the header sizes of UDP and of TCP (without options)?
explanation_en: The UDP header has only four 2-byte fields (source port, destination port, length, checksum) = 8 bytes. The TCP header has a minimum of 20 bytes because it carries sequence and acknowledgement numbers, flags and window size.

question_en: TCP prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver by using the:

options.en: Sliding window mechanism advertised by the receiver

explanation_en: The receiver advertises a window size indicating how much data it can buffer, and the sender limits unacknowledged data to that window; this is TCP flow control. Checksum is for error detection and TTL belongs to IP.

question_en: The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) is used to:

options.en: Find the IP address when only the MAC address is known
Find the MAC address of a host whose IP address is known
Find the IP address of a host whose domain name is known
Assign IP addresses automatically to hosts

explanation_en: ARP broadcasts 'who has this IP?' and the owner replies with its MAC address so a frame can be built. Name-to-IP is DNS, automatic assignment is DHCP and MAC-to-IP is the older RARP.

question_en: Which protocol–layer pairing (in the TCP/IP model) is INCORRECT?
explanation_en: UDP, like TCP, is a Transport-layer protocol. SMTP is an application protocol, IP works at the Internet layer, and Ethernet operates at the Network Access (link) layer.

question_en: Which routing protocol is used to exchange routes between different autonomous systems (for example, between ISPs) on the Internet?
explanation_en: Border Gateway Protocol is the exterior gateway protocol that connects autonomous systems. RIP and OSPF are interior protocols used within one organisation, and ARP is not a routing protocol at all.

question_en: In the Routing Information Protocol (RIP), a destination whose hop count is 16 is treated as:
explanation_en: RIP is a distance-vector protocol whose maximum valid hop count is 15; a metric of 16 means 'infinity', i.e. unreachable. This limit keeps RIP suitable only for small networks.

question_en: The ping utility checks whether a remote host is reachable by sending messages of which protocol?
explanation_en: ping sends ICMP Echo Request messages and waits for Echo Reply messages, reporting round-trip time and loss. It does not use TCP, DNS's UDP port or HTTP.

question_en: By default, a web server serving HTTPS pages listens on TCP port:
explanation_en: HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) uses well-known port 443. Port 80 is plain HTTP, 8080 is a common alternate HTTP port and 21 is FTP control.

question_en: The well-known port number of HTTP is:
explanation_en: HTTP servers listen on port 80 by default. Port 25 is SMTP, 110 is POP3 and 53 is DNS.

question_en: FTP uses two TCP connections. Which ports are used for the control connection and the data connection (active mode) respectively?
explanation_en: FTP sends commands over port 21 (control) and transfers file contents over port 20 (data) in active mode. 22/23 are SSH/Telnet and 69 is TFTP.

question_en: Match the protocol with its default port: SMTP, POP3, IMAP.
explanation_en: SMTP (sending mail) uses port 25, POP3 (downloading mail) uses 110 and IMAP (accessing mail on the server) uses 143.

question_en: DNS queries are normally sent to which port?
explanation_en: DNS uses port 53 (UDP for ordinary queries, TCP for zone transfers and large replies). 67 is DHCP server, 123 is NTP and 161 is SNMP.

question_en: Which pair of remote-login protocols and ports is correct?
explanation_en: SSH on port 22 encrypts the whole session, while Telnet on port 23 sends everything, including passwords, as clear text. That is why SSH has replaced Telnet for remote administration.

question_en: Port numbers are 16-bit values. The range 0–1023 is known as:
explanation_en: IANA classifies ports as well-known (0–1023, e.g. 80, 443), registered (1024–49151) and dynamic/ephemeral (49152–65535). Being 16-bit, there are 65,536 ports in total.

question_en: DHCP uses UDP ports 67 and 68, and SNMP uses UDP port 161. Which of the following also runs over UDP on port 69?
explanation_en: Trivial File Transfer Protocol is a simple, no-authentication file transfer protocol that uses UDP port 69. FTP uses TCP 20/21 and SFTP runs over SSH on TCP 22.

question_en: Which service translates a domain name such as www.education.delhi.gov.in into an IP address?
explanation_en: The Domain Name System resolves human-readable names to IP addresses. DHCP assigns IP addresses, FTP transfers files and ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses.

question_en: Which protocol is used to SEND e-mail from a mail client to a mail server and between mail servers?
explanation_en: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol is a 'push' protocol used for sending and relaying mail. POP3 and IMAP are used by clients to retrieve mail from the server.

question_en: Which protocol automatically assigns an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS server to a computer when it joins a network?
explanation_en: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol leases IP configuration to clients automatically, avoiding manual setup. DNS only resolves names.

question_en: HTTPS differs from HTTP mainly because HTTPS:

options.en: Does not need a web server
Can transfer only text, not images

explanation_en: HTTPS is HTTP carried inside an SSL/TLS encrypted channel, protecting data from eavesdropping and tampering and authenticating the server through a certificate. It still uses TCP.

question_en: A teacher reads her school e-mail on a laptop, a phone and a desktop and wants every folder and 'read' status to stay synchronised on all of them. The retrieval protocol best suited is:
explanation_en: IMAP keeps messages and folders on the server and synchronises state across devices. POP3 usually downloads and removes mail from the server, so the devices fall out of sync; SMTP only sends mail.

question_en: HTTP is called a 'stateless' protocol because:

options.en: It does not use any port number
It works without a TCP connection
It cannot carry images or video
The server does not retain information about previous requests from the same client

explanation_en: Each HTTP request is processed independently; the server keeps no memory of earlier requests. Websites therefore use cookies or sessions to remember logged-in users.

question_en: A browser displays the HTTP status code 404. This means:

options.en: The server had an internal error
The requested page was not found on the server

explanation_en: 404 Not Found is a client-error code meaning the resource does not exist at that URL. 200 means OK, 500 is Internal Server Error and 301 is Moved Permanently.

question_en: Which DNS resource record identifies the mail server responsible for accepting e-mail for a domain?
explanation_en: An MX (Mail Exchanger) record names the mail server for a domain. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, CNAME creates an alias and PTR is used for reverse lookup.

question_en: In the Domain Name System, the label '.in' in 'ncert.nic.in' is called a:
explanation_en: The right-most label is the top-level domain; '.in' is India's country-code TLD (ccTLD). Generic TLDs include .com, .org and .edu.

question_en: A firewall protects a network mainly by:

options.en: Converting digital signals to analog signals
Increasing the bandwidth of the Internet connection
Allowing or blocking traffic according to a set of security rules

explanation_en: A firewall (hardware or software) inspects incoming and outgoing traffic and permits or denies it based on rules such as IP address, port and protocol. Address assignment is DHCP's job and signal conversion is a modem's.

question_en: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) allows a teacher working from home to access the school server securely because it:

options.en: Creates an encrypted tunnel across the public Internet
Gives the laptop a faster processor
Connects directly by a dedicated physical cable
Removes the need for any password

explanation_en: A VPN encapsulates and encrypts traffic between the remote user and the private network, so the public Internet carries it privately. It still uses the ordinary Internet link, not a dedicated cable.

question_en: In symmetric-key cryptography such as AES:

options.en: A public key encrypts and a private key decrypts
No key is needed for decryption
Each message uses a key pair published in a directory
The same secret key is used for encryption and decryption

explanation_en: Symmetric algorithms (AES, DES) share one secret key between sender and receiver, making them fast but creating a key-distribution problem. Public/private key pairs are used in asymmetric systems such as RSA.

question_en: Using a Caesar cipher with a shift of 3, the plaintext word NET is encrypted as:
explanation_en: Each letter is moved three places forward: N→Q, E→H, T→W, giving QHW. OFU uses a shift of 1 and KBQ shifts backward by 3.

question_en: Alice wants to send Bob a message that only Bob can read, and also prove that she is the sender. She should:

options.en: Sign with her own private key and encrypt with Bob's public key
Encrypt with a shared key and sign with Bob's public key
Sign with her public key and encrypt with Bob's private key
Sign with Bob's private key and encrypt with her own public key

explanation_en: A digital signature is created with the sender's private key and verified with her public key, proving authorship. Confidentiality comes from encrypting with the receiver's public key, since only Bob's private key can decrypt it.

question_en: In network security, a DMZ (demilitarised zone) is best described as:

options.en: A separate subnet holding public-facing servers, isolated from the internal LAN by firewalls
A part of the LAN where no passwords are required
A wireless zone in which encryption is disabled
The range of private IP addresses reserved for routers

explanation_en: Web, mail and DNS servers that must be reachable from the Internet are placed in a DMZ so that if one is compromised the attacker still faces a firewall before reaching the internal network.

question_en: Wi-Fi wireless LANs are based on which IEEE standard family?
explanation_en: Wi-Fi is the IEEE 802.11 family (a/b/g/n/ac/ax). 802.3 is wired Ethernet, 802.15 covers wireless PANs such as Bluetooth, and 802.5 is Token Ring.

question_en: Bluetooth is primarily a technology for which type of network?
explanation_en: Bluetooth connects devices such as earphones, keyboards and phones over a short range (typically about 10 m) in the 2.4 GHz band, forming a PAN.

question_en: The name of a Wi-Fi network that appears in the list of available networks on a phone is called its:
explanation_en: The Service Set Identifier is the human-readable network name broadcast by an access point. The WPA key is the password, and MAC/IP are device addresses.

question_en: Which Wi-Fi security protocol is considered the weakest and should no longer be used?
explanation_en: Wired Equivalent Privacy has serious flaws and can be cracked in minutes. WPA2 with AES and the newer WPA3 are the recommended options.

question_en: Wired Ethernet traditionally used CSMA/CD, but Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA because:

options.en: A wireless station cannot reliably detect collisions while transmitting, so it tries to avoid them
CSMA/CA gives higher speed than CSMA/CD on cables
Wi-Fi uses token passing instead of carrier sensing

explanation_en: A radio cannot listen while it transmits and may not hear hidden stations, so collision detection is impractical. Wi-Fi therefore uses collision avoidance with random back-off and optional RTS/CTS.

question_en: In the URL https://www.cbse.gov.in/results/index.html, the part 'https' is the:
explanation_en: A URL is made of the scheme (https), the host or domain (www.cbse.gov.in) and the path (/results/index.html). '.in' alone is the top-level domain.

question_en: Small pieces of data that a website stores in the user's browser to remember login status or preferences are called:
explanation_en: Cookies are small text files sent by a website and stored by the browser, then returned with later requests so the stateless HTTP protocol can 'remember' the user. Bookmarks are saved links chosen by the user.

question_en: A company such as BSNL or Airtel that provides customers with access to the Internet is known as a(n):
explanation_en: An ISP connects homes and organisations to the Internet. A registrar sells domain names and an Internet Exchange Point is where ISPs interconnect.

question_en: A school's private network that uses Internet technologies (web pages, e-mail) but is accessible only to its own staff is called a(n):
explanation_en: An intranet is an organisation-only network built on Internet protocols. An extranet extends controlled access to selected outsiders such as suppliers, and Ethernet is a LAN wiring standard.

question_en: A 100 MB file is downloaded over a link with an effective speed of 8 Mbps. Ignoring overheads, the download time is approximately (take 1 MB = 8 Mb):
explanation_en: 100 MB = 100 × 8 = 800 megabits. Time = 800 Mb ÷ 8 Mbps = 100 s. Dividing 100 by 8 gives 12.5 s, the trap of forgetting that link speed is in bits and file size in bytes.
